title: Rate limiting (fixed window, sliding window, concurrency)
hook: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can send in a time window. ASP.NET Core 7+ ships built-in middleware with fixed, sliding, token-bucket, and concurrency limiters — return 429 Too Many Requests before your database does.

blocks.text: Rate limiting protects APIs from abuse, accidental retry storms, and noisy neighbors after large customer onboarding. Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting provides partition keys (IP, user id, API key client_id), multiple algorithms, and OnRejected callbacks for Problem Details responses. Limiters run early in the pipeline — typically after routing so endpoint metadata can select policies. Distributed rate limiting requires a shared store (Redis) when multiple API instances must enforce one global budget.

entries.plainDefinition: Allows N requests per fixed time slice (e.g. 100 per minute starting at :00).
Counts requests in a rolling interval — smoother than fixed window burst at boundary.
Tokens refill at steady rate; burst allowed up to bucket capacity.
Caps simultaneous in-flight requests per partition — not requests per second.

blocks.text: OWASP API Security Top 10 lists unrestricted resource consumption (API4) — rate limiting is the first line of defense alongside pagination caps and body size limits. After onboarding a tenant that runs aggressive integration tests, fixed-window limiters may allow 200 requests at 12:00:59 and 12:01:00 (boundary burst). Senior engineers explain algorithm tradeoffs, Retry-After headers, and per-tenant vs global partitions.

blocks.title: 429 is not authentication
blocks.body: Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After when quota exceeded. Do not confuse with 401/403. Log partition key and policy name for support tickets — never log raw API keys.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Select partition key
items.body: IP address, authenticated user id, or API key client_id from claims.

items.title: Acquire permit
items.body: Limiter algorithm decrements quota for this partition.

items.title: Rejected
items.body: OnRejected writes 429, Retry-After, and optional Problem Details.

items.title: Accepted
items.body: Request continues to auth, caching, and endpoint.

items.title: Release (concurrency)
items.body: Concurrency limiter releases slot when response completes.

snippet.label: Register multiple limiter policies
snippet.explanation: Fixed window is simplest but boundary-bursts. Sliding window smooths spikes. Concurrency caps long-running exports — different axis than requests/minute.

snippet.label: Partition by authenticated tenant after onboarding
snippet.explanation: Large customers get tenant_id claim — partition by tenant not shared IP (NAT). Fallback to IP for anonymous health probes.

snippet.label: Token bucket for bursty mobile clients
snippet.explanation: Token bucket allows short bursts (app launch sync) while maintaining average rate — better UX than strict fixed window for mobile.

snippet.label: Diagnostics — log rejections with partition key
snippet.explanation: Track 429 rate per tenant after onboarding — spike may mean integration misconfigured retry loop, not attack.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Rate limiting after expensive middleware (auth + DB before 429). Same global limit for health checks and heavy exports. No Retry-After header (clients exponential-backoff blindly). In-memory limiter on multi-instance farm without shared Redis — each pod allows full quota.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: metric http.server.requests{status=429} per route and tenant. Compare fixed vs sliding — if 429s cluster at minute boundaries, switch to sliding or token bucket. For farm-wide limits, implement Redis-backed PartitionedRateLimiter or Azure API Management front door. dotnet-counters does not expose rate limits — use app metrics and load test with k6 verifying 429 ratio.

blocks.title: Algorithm selection
rows: Tuning token limit requires load tests
Does not limit requests per second

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Cannot explain fixed-window boundary burst. Saying rate limiting replaces authentication. No mention of distributed store when running ten pods. Using concurrency limiter when you meant requests-per-minute.

interviewTakeaways: Built-in RateLimiter (.NET 7+) supports fixed, sliding, token bucket, and concurrency algorithms with partition keys.
When not to use as sole defense: authenticated abuse needs per-user quotas; DDoS needs edge/WAF not app-tier limiter alone.
Production tip: partition by tenant_id after onboarding; Retry-After on 429; Redis for farm-wide counts.

60s: Acquire permit early in pipeline per partition. Fixed window resets at boundary — can double burst. Sliding rolls. Token bucket allows burst. Concurrency caps in-flight work. 429 with Retry-After.
Follow-up: how would you implement global rate limit across ten Kubernetes pods?
commonPitfalls: Saying '100 req/min fixed window stops all abuse' gets you rejected — clients can send 200 at minute rollover.
Per-pod in-memory limiter on scaled deployment — effective limit is N × PermitLimit.
Strong answer: 'Sliding window per tenant_id in Redis partition; concurrency limit on export endpoint; 429 with Retry-After; alert when one tenant hits 429 constantly after onboarding.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Default store is in-memory Map like fixed window per IP — same multi-instance multiplication problem without Redis.
ThrottlerModule uses TTL + limit similar to fixed window; custom storage needed for Redis farm-wide.
